planting.note: Set dormant pseudobulbs just below the surface of a free-draining, humus-rich mix in very early spring before new growth emerges; keep barely moist until roots form, then water and feed through summer before withholding water for a dry winter rest.

directions: Pleione yunnanensis is a deciduous, pseudobulbous ground orchid from mossy rocks and tree bases in the forests of Yunnan and northern Vietnam, flowering in spring with solitary pink to rose-purple blooms marked with darker spots on the fringed lip, appearing before the new leaf unfurls. In cultivation it is grown like other hardy Pleiones, in shallow pans or a sheltered, humus-rich woodland pocket in dappled shade, with generous moisture and feeding through the leafy growing season followed by a cool, dry winter rest. Where winters are wet it is safest grown in an unheated alpine house or cold frame and only planted out in mild, well-drained shade gardens. Propagation is by the small offset bulbils that form around the base of each flowered pseudobulb.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines

planting.note: Plant dormant pseudobulbs just below the surface of an open, moss-and-grit mix in earliest spring; this high-altitude species is among the hardiest Pleiones and tolerates cooler, more exposed woodland positions than most relatives.

directions: Pleione hookeriana grows wild at high elevation across the Himalaya and southwest China, often rooted in moss and leaf litter under dwarf rhododendron scrub where winters are long and cold, making it one of the hardiest species in its genus. Solitary pink to purplish-pink flowers with a spotted, fringed lip appear on short stems in spring just ahead of the single thin leaf, and the whole plant dies back completely by autumn. It is best grown in a shallow pan of gritty, humus-rich compost in a cool, lightly shaded spot, watered and fed generously during active growth, then kept nearly dry and cold once the leaf yellows. Offsets that form at the base of the spent pseudobulb are the usual means of increase.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines

planting.note: Pot dormant pseudobulbs shallowly in a sharply draining, mineral-heavy mix in spring to mimic the thin moss and humus pockets of its native limestone cliffs; water and feed through summer leaf growth, then keep dry and cool over winter.

directions: Pleione scopulorum takes its name from its habitat on limestone cliff ledges in Yunnan, where it roots in thin moss and humus over rock rather than in deep soil. Pale pink to near-white flowers with a yellow-blotched, fringed lip open in spring on short stems, close to the ground, before the single new leaf expands fully. In cultivation it prefers a shallow, very free-draining gritty compost and a sheltered, lightly shaded site that recreates the quick-drying, mineral-rich conditions of its cliff-ledge origin, with a strict dry winter rest once dormant. It is well suited to an alpine trough, raised scree bed, or cold frame in climates where winter wet would otherwise rot the resting bulbs. Increase is from the small bulbils produced at the base of mature pseudobulbs.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Alpines

planting.note: Plant dormant pseudobulbs shallowly in a gritty, humus-rich mix in early spring on a shaded, mossy rock ledge or in a pan; this lower-elevation species tolerates slightly warmer summers than most Chinese Pleiones but still needs a dry winter rest.

directions: Pleione chekiangensis is native to mossy rock faces and shaded forest boulders in Zhejiang province, growing at lower elevations than many of its Chinese relatives and tolerating somewhat warmer, more humid summers as a result. Rose-purple flowers with a frilled, spotted lip open singly on each pseudobulb in spring, just before or alongside the emerging leaf. It is grown much like other hardy Pleiones, rooted shallowly in a gritty, moisture-retentive medium on a shaded rock garden ledge or in a pan, watered freely while in leaf and kept dry once dormant. Clumps slowly bulk up from offset bulbils and can be divided and repotted every few years as the pseudobulbs crowd their container.

planting.note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring once the ground has warmed, into humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade; this is the most cold-hardy Bletilla, tolerating colder winters than the familiar Bletilla striata without extra mulch.

directions: Bletilla sinica occurs across a broad swath of north-central China, from Gansu and Shaanxi to Henan and Sichuan, growing at higher latitude and altitude than the more familiar Bletilla striata and proving noticeably tougher in winter cold. It forms clumps of narrow, pleated leaves topped in late spring by sprays of smaller, pale rose-purple flowers held above the foliage. Grow it in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a lightly shaded woodland or border setting, mulching new plantings their first winter until an established clump builds cold tolerance. It is a useful substitute for gardeners in colder zones who want Bletilla's grassy foliage and orchid flowers without the winter protection striata often needs, and is increased by dividing dormant pseudobulb clusters in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions with several pseudobulbs in spring into rich, well-drained humus soil in deep to dappled shade; this evergreen species does not go fully dormant and needs frost-free winters or a sheltered microclimate.

directions: Calanthe sylvatica is an evergreen terrestrial orchid of humid forest floors across Madagascar, the Mascarene Islands, and parts of tropical Asia, forming broad, pleated, glossy leaves from stout pseudobulbs. Tall, arching spikes of rose-purple to magenta flowers with a prominent spurred lip rise well above the foliage in winter and spring, making a bold statement in a shaded subtropical border. It needs constant warmth, high humidity, and rich, evenly moist but free-draining soil in deep to dappled shade, and does not tolerate frost or extended dry spells. Where winters are mild it makes a striking shade-garden perennial; elsewhere it is best grown in a large container and moved under cover before cold weather arrives, and is readily increased by dividing congested clumps.
sources: Flora of Madagascar and the Comoros

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions shallowly in spring into humus-rich, constantly moist but free-draining woodland soil in deep shade; in frost-free climates grow outdoors as a groundcover, elsewhere pot up for a shaded terrarium or cool greenhouse.

directions: Goodyera velutina is a creeping evergreen jewel orchid from the forest floors of Japan, Taiwan, and parts of China, prized for its dark, velvety leaves etched with a pale, luminous midrib stripe rather than for its small, unshowy greenish-white flower spikes produced in autumn. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a low, glossy mat in the deepest, most humid shade a woodland garden can offer, needing constantly moist, humus-rich soil and protection from drying wind. Where winters bring hard frost it is best grown as a terrarium or cool greenhouse groundcover rather than planted outdoors, since the foliage is easily damaged by cold or by direct sun. Clumps are easily increased by cutting and replanting rooted sections of the creeping stem.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring into sharply draining, calcareous, humus-poor soil at a woodland edge or open scrub margin; this species dislikes the rich, damp woodland soil favored by most shade orchids and instead wants lean, lime-rich ground.

directions: Epipactis atrorubens, the dark red helleborine, is a cold-hardy European terrestrial orchid of chalk and limestone grassland, old quarries, dunes, and the sunnier, drier margins of open woodland, ranging as far north as Scandinavia. In early to midsummer it produces upright spikes of small, dusky wine-red to purple-brown flowers with a sweet, vanilla-like fragrance that attracts bees and wasps. Unlike most shade-garden orchids it prefers lean, sharply drained, lime-rich soil and resents the rich, consistently damp humus that suits woodland species, making it best suited to a chalky rock garden, scree bed, or the lightly shaded edge of a limestone woodland path. Established clumps persist for years and can be gently divided, though plants establish most reliably from nursery-propagated stock rather than wild collection.
sources: Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland
